title: Binary Search with an Executable Trace
purpose: Programming fixture for a complete algorithm, an honest execution trace, absent-target termination, exact comparison bounds, delayed retrieval practice, and deterministic caption alignment.

learner.audience: Beginning programmers who understand arrays, comparison, and loops.

objectives.statement: Explain the inclusive candidate-interval invariant and why ascending sort order is required.
criteria: Keeps every possible match inside the interval
Does not claim binary search works on arbitrary unsorted input

objectives.statement: Read and apply complete iterative binary-search pseudocode.
criteria: Returns not found after the loop

objectives.statement: Trace low, mid, high, and the compared value until target 44 is found at index 6.
criteria: Does not invent a post-match singleton interval

objectives.statement: Trace an absent target and empty input without out-of-bounds access.
criteria: Performs no access for an empty list

objectives.statement: Distinguish halvings from value probes and compare binary search with linear scan.
criteria: States 10 halvings to one candidate for 1,024 values

objectives.statement: Recall whether binary search may discard half of an unsorted array.
criteria: Commits to an answer before feedback
Explains why sorted order justifies elimination

claims.statement: The discard step is valid only when the searched values are sorted in the order assumed by the comparisons.
If the target exists, each unsuccessful update keeps at least one matching index inside the inclusive interval [low, high].

A complete iterative implementation initializes both bounds, loops while low is at most high, uses a floored midpoint, guards equality and order branches, excludes mid after a miss, and returns not found after the loop.
For [3,8,12,17,23,31,44,58,72], target 44 is found at index 6 from interval [5,8] after probes at indices 4 and 6.
For [3,8,12,17,23,31,44,58,72], absent target 50 probes indices 4, 6, and 7, then terminates with low 7 and high 6.
For 1,024 values, ten halvings leave one candidate and the worst case uses up to 11 value probes.
Iterative binary search uses O(log n) time and O(1) auxiliary space, while linear scan can use O(n) time.

scenes.title: First, check the promise
scenes.narration: Binary search can discard a side only because these values are sorted in ascending order. On arbitrary unsorted input, the target could still be on either side of the midpoint.
scenes.visualIntent: Show the ordered array 3, 8, 12, 17, 23, 31, 44, 58, 72. Label ascending order as the prerequisite; contrast it with a crossed-out shuffled array.
scenes.captionText: Prerequisite: values sorted in ascending order
scenes.accessibilityDescription: A sorted nine-item array is marked valid, while a shuffled array is marked invalid for ordinary binary search.

scenes.title: Keep every possible match
scenes.narration: Low and high form an inclusive candidate interval. If the target exists, at least one matching index remains inside that interval after every unsuccessful update.
scenes.visualIntent: Bracket the inclusive interval and retain possible indices. Use labels and strike marks, not color alone, to distinguish candidates from discarded positions.
scenes.captionText: Invariant: a possible match remains in [low, high]
scenes.accessibilityDescription: Low and high brackets surround all remaining candidate positions in the sorted array.

scenes.title: Run the complete loop
scenes.narration: Initialize low and high. While low is no greater than high, floor the midpoint, return on equality, move low after a smaller value, or move high after a larger value. Return not found only after the loop.
scenes.visualIntent: Display every supplied pseudocode line in order. Highlight one guarded branch at a time and keep the final NOT_FOUND return visibly outside the loop.
scenes.captionText:
low = 0; high = length(values) - 1
while low <= high do
mid = low + floor((high - low) / 2)
if values[mid] == target then return mid
if values[mid] < target then low = mid + 1
else high = mid - 1
end while
return NOT_FOUND
scenes.accessibilityDescription: Complete iterative pseudocode is exposed in a deterministic text reading order, with loop boundaries and branch guards announced.

scenes.title: Find 44 without inventing a state
scenes.narration: Start at interval zero through eight. Index four holds 23, so low becomes five. The next interval is five through eight. Index six holds 44, so return six immediately. The interval at return is still five through eight.
scenes.visualIntent: Show exactly two rows: [0,8], mid 4, value 23, low becomes 5; then [5,8], mid 6, value 44, return 6. End the trace on the equality return without any further boundary update.
scenes.accessibilityDescription: A two-row state table lists low, mid, high, compared value, and action; the final interval is five through eight.

scenes.title: Prove 50 is absent
scenes.narration: For target 50, probe values 23, 44, and 58 at indices four, six, and seven. High then becomes six while low is seven. The candidate interval is empty, so return not found.
scenes.visualIntent: Show rows [0,8], [5,8], and [7,8], followed by the explicit terminating bounds low 7 and high 6. Mark every discarded region.
scenes.accessibilityDescription: A three-row state table ends with low seven greater than high six and announces not found.

scenes.title: Ten halvings, eleven probes
scenes.narration: With 1,024 values, ten halvings reduce the candidates to one, but that last candidate still needs a probe. The worst case is therefore 11 value probes, versus as many as 1,024 for linear scan.
scenes.visualIntent: Animate the count 1024, 512, 256, 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, then add a separately labeled final probe. Compare 11 with 1024.
scenes.accessibilityDescription: A labeled halving sequence reaches one candidate, followed by a distinct final-probe marker and a comparison with linear scan.

scenes.title: Commit before feedback
scenes.narration: Quick check. Can ordinary binary search safely discard half of an unsorted array? Choose yes or no, and say why. Commit to your answer before the next scene.
scenes.visualIntent: Show only the question and two choices, Yes and No. Do not display, highlight, narrate, or imply the answer in this scene.
scenes.captionText: Can binary search safely discard half of an unsorted array? Yes or No?
scenes.accessibilityDescription: A question asks whether ordinary binary search can discard half of an unsorted array; Yes and No are unselected choices.

scenes.title: Answer: no
scenes.narration: No. Sorted order is the evidence that a midpoint comparison eliminates one side. Without that order, a target could be anywhere, so discarding half is not justified.
scenes.visualIntent: Now reveal and explain No. Reuse the sorted-versus-shuffled comparison and explicitly connect the answer to the prerequisite.
scenes.captionText: No — sorted order justifies eliminating one side
scenes.accessibilityDescription: The No choice is selected only after the separate question scene, followed by a text explanation.

scenes.title: The reliable checklist
scenes.narration: Recap: require sorted values, keep an inclusive candidate interval, return immediately on equality, exclude the midpoint after a miss, return not found when low exceeds high, and remember that 1,024 values can need 11 probes.
scenes.visualIntent: Build a six-item checklist that retrieves the prerequisite, invariant, branch behavior, absent case, and exact 1,024-value bound.
scenes.captionText: Sorted • inclusive bounds • guarded branches • empty interval • 11 probes
scenes.accessibilityDescription: A six-item text checklist summarizes the prerequisite, algorithm, termination rule, and comparison bound.

qualityAssertions.description: The displayed pseudocode includes initialization, loop and branch guards, floored midpoint arithmetic, boundary updates, and the not-found return.
expected: if values[mid] == target then return mid
if values[mid] < target then low = mid + 1

qualityAssertions.description: The authored found trace agrees with execution and does not fabricate a post-match interval.
The absent-target trace reaches an empty interval without an out-of-bounds access.
Empty input executes no element access and returns not found.
The lesson distinguishes the number of halvings from the worst-case number of value probes.
Learners receive a genuine retrieval opportunity before answer feedback appears.
SRT and VTT offsets use cumulative authored scene durations, not cumulative raw narration durations.
Every factual claim has exact local support.
Highlighted code is also exposed in a deterministic textual reading order.
Trace visuals reflow rather than crop on portrait output.

provenance.notes: Algorithm, traces, exact comparison bound, delayed retrieval practice, and caption clock are locally authored and guarded by explicit assertions.
